charts.title: Loss Ratio vs Expense Ratio (Combined Operating Ratio)
charts.annotation: Loss ratio + expense ratio = combined operating ratio; below 100% means the underwriting book itself is profitable before investment income.

charts.annotation: Regulatory minimum is 100% under C-ROSS II; PICC P&C has run 229-284% over FY2018-H1 FY2026.

charts.title: Net Income vs Free Cash Flow vs Owner FCF
charts.annotation: Owner FCF, where shown, is the DCF's series after SBC, interest income and lease principal.

balanceSheet.title: Balance sheet
balanceSheet.content:
Shareholders' equity is assets less liabilities; plotted against total liabilities to show leverage.

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: equity that grows only through revaluations or share issues is not the same as retained earnings.

What to watch:

  • Liabilities growing faster than equity
  • Goodwill share of equity after acquisitions

cashDebt.title: Cash and debt
cashDebt.content:
Cash & equivalents against total borrowings (leases excluded unless noted).

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: the DCF's net-debt bridge uses these balances at the latest balance-sheet date.

What to watch:

  • Net debt trend versus EBITDA
  • Refinancing dates and covenants in the filings

epsDps.title: EPS and dividends
epsDps.content:
EPS is net income per share; DPS is the cash dividend paid per share. Both are in major currency units.

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: the payout ratio (DPS / EPS) shows how much of earnings is returned versus reinvested.

What to watch:

  • EPS growth versus net income growth (dilution)
  • Dividends funded from earnings, not debt

fcf.title: Free cash flow
fcf.content:
Reported FCF is operating cash flow less capital expenditure. Owner FCF (from the DCF) further deducts stock-based compensation, interest income and lease principal -- the cash an owner could actually take out.

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: the gap between net income and owner FCF is the earnings-quality question the valuation is built on.

What to watch:

  • FCF persistently below net income
  • Working-capital swings inflating one year's FCF

margins.title: Margins
margins.content:
Gross margin is revenue less cost of revenue; operating margin deducts operating expenses; net margin is after interest and tax.

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: the spread between gross and operating margin is the cost of running the business; a widening spread with flat gross margin means opex is growing faster than sales.

What to watch:

  • Direction of operating margin over several years, not one
  • One-offs (impairments, disposals) that distort net margin

ocfCapex.title: Operating cash flow and CapEx
ocfCapex.content:
Operating cash flow is cash generated by operations; CapEx is cash invested in fixed and intangible assets.

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: CapEx here is shown as stored (sign convention varies by ticker); the DCF splits it into stay-in-business and growth where disclosed.

What to watch:

  • CapEx rising faster than revenue
  • OCF that diverges from EBITDA

profit.title: Profit lines
profit.content:
Gross profit is revenue less cost of revenue; operating income deducts operating expenses; net income is after interest, tax and one-offs.

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: the three lines together show where margin is made and lost between the top line and the bottom.

What to watch:

  • Operating income growing slower than gross profit (opex creep)
  • Net income far from operating income (interest, tax, one-offs)

revenue.title: Revenue
revenue.content:
Revenue is the top line: what customers paid for goods and services in the period, before any costs.

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: the growth rate matters more than the level; compare it with the DCF's base-case growth path below.

What to watch:

  • Acceleration or deceleration in YoY growth
  • Whether growth is organic or acquired
  • Interim rows show seasonality

underwritingRatios.title: Loss ratio and expense ratio
underwritingRatios.content:
The loss ratio is claims incurred as a percentage of net earned premium; the expense ratio is underwriting and administrative expenses as a percentage of premium. Added together they equal the combined operating ratio (already a headline KPI above): below 100% means the insurance book is profitable on underwriting alone, before any investment income.

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: the combined ratio improved from 98.8% (FY2024) to 97.5% (FY2025) to 94.0% (H1 FY2026) on regulator-led 'underwriting as filed' discipline in motor and 'comprehensive governance' in non-motor lines -- this chart shows whether that came from better pricing (loss ratio) or cost control (expense ratio), and NEV (new-energy-vehicle) insurance, now over 30% market share and growing ~31% YoY, is a loss-ratio risk since EV claims run more expensive than traditional motor.

What to watch:

  • Loss ratio creeping up even as the combined ratio looks stable (expense cuts masking claims deterioration)
  • NEV and liability-line claims experience versus mature motor
  • Large/catastrophe events distorting a single period's loss ratio

solvencyRatio.title: Comprehensive solvency margin ratio
solvencyRatio.content:
The comprehensive solvency margin ratio is a Chinese insurer's regulatory capital-adequacy measure under C-ROSS (China Risk-Oriented Solvency System) II -- actual recognised capital divided by minimum capital required for the risks on the book. The regulatory minimum is 100%; most insurers run well above it as a buffer against a capital-markets shock or a reserve strengthening.

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: the ratio sits at 237.2% (comprehensive) / 213.8% (core) as of H1 FY2026, comfortably above the minimum and giving PICC P&C balance-sheet capacity and preferential reinsurance terms versus smaller competitors; it dropped from ~280% (FY2019-21) to ~230% (FY2022 onward) on a C-ROSS II recalibration, not a capital event, and has since been stable. This is the single number a regulator would act on first if it fell -- dividend capacity and growth appetite both depend on it staying well clear of 100%.

What to watch:

  • A sustained decline toward the regulatory minimum, not a one-period dip
  • Regulatory recalibration of risk factors (e.g., for equities), which can move the ratio without any change in the underlying business
  • Dividend payout relative to capital generation -- a rising payout funded by solvency headroom rather than earnings

sbc.title: Stock-based compensation and share count
sbc.content:
Stock-based comp is the expense of equity awards; shares outstanding shows the dilution it causes net of buybacks.

For PICC Property and Casualty Company Limited: the DCF charges SBC as a cash cost and holds the share count flat, so this chart is the check on that assumption.

What to watch:

  • Share count rising while buybacks are advertised
  • SBC as a percentage of revenue
